track.name: System design case studies
track.blurb: Backend and distributed system design prompts answered the way strong candidates do: scoped, estimated, drawn, and defended under follow-ups.

questions.q: How do you structure a 45-minute backend system design interview?
questions.answer:
**I announce a plan and stick to it: requirements (about 5-7 minutes), quick estimates that drive decisions, API and data model, a simple high-level design traced end to end, then the second half on two or three deep dives chosen with the interviewer, and a short wrap-up on bottlenecks and failure modes.**

**Timeline I aim for:**

| Minutes | Step | What is on the board |
|---|---|---|
| 0-7 | Requirements | Functional list, non-functional targets, explicit out-of-scope |
| 7-11 | Estimation | Peak QPS, read/write ratio, storage, hot set, each with a conclusion |
| 11-18 | API + data model | 3-6 endpoints, entities with keys and partition key |
| 18-27 | High-level design | 6-10 boxes, write path and read path narrated |
| 27-42 | Deep dives | The 2-3 hardest problems for this product |
| 42-45 | Wrap-up | Bottlenecks, failure modes, what I would build first |

**Requirements** are where I earn the right to design. I ask about core use cases, scale (DAU, peak), latency and availability targets, consistency needs (where staleness is acceptable), and durability. I write out-of-scope items explicitly, which invites the interviewer to redirect early instead of at minute 30.

**Estimation** is only useful if it changes something. "Writes are 200 per second, so one primary is fine; reads are 30k per second, so we cache; images are 2 TB a day, so object storage and CDN." Three decisions in two minutes.

**API and data model** before boxes, because access patterns decide the store. I say the partition key out loud and why.

**High-level design**: the simplest design that meets every functional requirement. Then I trace a request: "a post goes here, emits this event, these workers do X; a read hits this cache and falls back to Y." If a box has no reason, I delete it.

**Deep dives**: I name the candidates ("the interesting parts are fan-out for celebrities and cache consistency; which would you like?") and run each as problem, options, trade-off, decision, failure mode.

**Throughout**, I check in at transitions and glance at the clock. If the interviewer pulls me into a deep dive early, I follow, because they are telling me where the points are, and I come back to finish the end-to-end picture briefly afterwards.
followUps: What do you do if the interviewer interrupts and wants to go deep early?
How do you decide which deep dives to pick?
What do you cut when you are running out of time?
mistakes: Weak answers start drawing boxes before agreeing on requirements and scale.
Weak answers spend 15 minutes on estimation that leads to no decision.
Weak answers never trace a read and a write path, so it is unclear the design works.
Weak answers leave no time for deep dives, which carry most of the senior signal.

questions.q: Walk me through a back-of-envelope estimate for a service with 100 million daily active users.
questions.answer:
**I state assumptions, round aggressively (a day is about 10^5 seconds), and compute four things: peak QPS split into reads and writes, storage growth, bandwidth, and the memory needed for the hot set. Then I say what each number means for the design.**

**Assumptions** (say them out loud, the interviewer can correct them): 100M DAU; each user does 10 reads and 1 write a day; average object 1 KB; 10% of writes carry a 300 KB image; peak is 3x average.

```text
Reads:    10^8 x 10 = 10^9/day   / 10^5 s = 10^4 QPS avg -> 3 x 10^4 peak
Writes:   10^8 x 1  = 10^8/day   / 10^5 s = 10^3 QPS avg -> 3 x 10^3 peak
Ratio:    10:1 read heavy

Storage (text):   10^8 x 1 KB    = 100 GB/day  -> ~36 TB/year
Storage (images): 10^7 x 300 KB  = 3 TB/day    -> ~1 PB/year
Egress (reads):   3 x 10^4 x 1 KB = 30 MB/s of metadata at peak
                  plus images served from CDN

Cache: 20% of daily reads are for "hot" objects -> cache the top objects
       e.g. 10^7 hot objects x 1 KB = 10 GB -> fits a small Redis cluster
```

**Conclusions I would say:**
- 3,000 writes per second is fine for a sharded relational or wide-column store; a single primary may struggle with that plus indexes, so plan to shard by user id.
- Reads at 30k per second with a 10:1 ratio justify a cache layer and read replicas.
- Images dominate storage by 30x, so they go to object storage behind a CDN and never through the API servers.
- 36 TB of text a year means the database must be partitioned within the first year or two.

**Useful constants:** 1 million per day is about 12 per second; 1 KB x 1 billion is 1 TB; a year is about 3 x 10^7 seconds; 99.9% availability allows about 43 minutes of downtime a month.

**What interviewers look for** is not precision. They want assumptions stated, consistent units, peak considered, and numbers that lead to decisions. If a number does not change the design (the data fits on one machine), I say so in one sentence and move on.
followUps: How would the estimate change for a write-heavy product like logging?
How do you estimate the cache size?
Why use 10^5 seconds per day?
mistakes: Weak answers compute numbers without stating assumptions first.
Weak answers forget peak traffic and design for the average.
Weak answers never draw a conclusion from the numbers.
Weak answers mix up bits and bytes or GB and TB by orders of magnitude.

questions.q: What separates a senior system design answer from a mid-level one?
questions.answer:
**A mid-level answer produces a reasonable design that works. A senior answer drives the conversation, finds the hardest problems without being prompted, quantifies trade-offs against the requirements, and covers how the system fails, is operated and evolves.**

**Concretely, the differences I aim to show:**

| Dimension | Mid-level | Senior |
|---|---|---|
| Scoping | Asks some questions | Pins numbers and consistency needs that change the design, parks scope explicitly |
| Design | Standard components | Simplest design that meets requirements; justifies every box |
| Depth | Explains components when asked | Picks the 2-3 real risks (celebrity fan-out, hot keys, unknown payment outcomes) and goes deep |
| Trade-offs | One option | Two or three options compared, decision tied to a requirement, cost stated |
| Failure | Mentions replication | Walks through node, zone and dependency failures; what degrades, what is lost |
| Operations | Rarely | Monitoring (SLOs, key metrics), rollout, migration, capacity, cost |
| Communication | Responds | Leads, checks in, adapts when steered |

**Examples of senior phrasing:**
- "I'll use fan-out on write for most users but not for accounts above about a million followers; the cost is a read-time merge, which is small because users follow few celebrities."
- "This is at-least-once with idempotent consumers. Exactly-once delivery is not achievable across the network; the dedup table gives us exactly-once effects."
- "If the cache cluster loses a node, we will see a miss storm on the database. I'd add request coalescing and keep the database sized to survive a 30% miss rate."
- "I'd ship the simple version first, measure, and only shard when we cross about 70% of a primary's write capacity."

**Disagreement**: when the interviewer challenges a choice, a senior candidate neither caves instantly nor digs in. They restate the trade-off, ask what requirement the interviewer has in mind, and either defend with reasoning or adapt.

**Staff level** adds evolution and organisation: which parts of the system will change in two years, how teams own components, migration paths from today's architecture, and where the design bets on assumptions that should be validated early.
followUps: How do you show operational maturity in a whiteboard interview?
What does a staff-level answer add on top?
How do you handle an interviewer who disagrees with your choice?
mistakes: Weak answers equate seniority with naming more technologies.
Weak answers wait for the interviewer to find the hard problems.
Weak answers present choices as obvious instead of as trade-offs.
Weak answers ignore operations: rollout, monitoring, failure and cost.

questions.q: How do you decide between SQL and NoSQL in a system design interview?
questions.answer:
**I decide from the access patterns and consistency needs, not from fashion. If I need transactions, constraints and flexible queries at moderate scale, I pick a relational database. If the dominant access is "fetch by key or key range" at very high write volume and I can live with limited queries, a key-value or wide-column store fits better.**

**Questions I ask myself:**
1. **What are the queries?** "Messages in conversation X after sequence N" is a key-range scan, ideal for a wide-column store partitioned by conversation. "Orders by customer joined with items, filtered by status" wants SQL.
2. **Do I need multi-row transactions?** Payments, ledgers, inventory: yes, so relational (or a distributed SQL database like Spanner or CockroachDB).
3. **What is the write volume?** Thousands per second is comfortable for a well-indexed Postgres primary; hundreds of thousands per second of appends suggests a partitioned store designed for it (Cassandra, ScyllaDB, DynamoDB).
4. **How will it grow?** Can a relational database be sharded by a natural key (tenant, user)? Often yes, and many large companies run sharded MySQL or Postgres (YouTube's Vitess is the classic example).
5. **Consistency**: is eventual consistency acceptable for this data?

**Typical choices in case studies:**

| Data | Store | Why |
|---|---|---|
| Payments, ledger | Relational / distributed SQL | Transactions, invariants |
| URL mappings | KV or sharded SQL | Pure key lookup |
| Chat messages | Wide-column | Append + range scan by conversation |
| Timelines | Redis lists | In-memory, capped, rebuildable |
| Driver locations | In-memory geo index | Ephemeral, write heavy |
| Search | Inverted index | Text matching, ranking |

**The partition key is the real decision.** In any distributed store, queries that include the partition key are cheap; queries that do not become scatter-gather across shards. So I name the key and check every hot query against it.

**What I avoid saying:** "NoSQL scales and SQL doesn't." Both scale with partitioning; the difference is what you give up (joins, cross-partition transactions) and what you get (predictable performance for key-based access at huge volume).
followUps: When would you shard a relational database rather than switch to NoSQL?
What does a wide-column store give you for chat messages?
How do secondary indexes behave in a partitioned store?
mistakes: Weak answers pick NoSQL because it 'scales' without describing the access pattern.
Weak answers ignore transactions and constraints where money or inventory is involved.
Weak answers forget that relational databases can be sharded and replicated.
Weak answers do not mention the partition key at all.

questions.q: How do you handle a hot key or hot partition in a design?
questions.answer:
**A single hot key cannot be fixed by adding shards, because one key lives on one shard. I absorb hot reads with replication or local caches, spread hot writes by splitting the key into sub-keys that are aggregated later, and detect hot keys with per-key metrics so mitigations can switch on automatically.**

**Where hot keys appear:** a viral short link, a celebrity's profile or recent posts, a flash-sale product's inventory, a like counter on a popular post, a time-based partition key where all new writes hit "today".

**Hot reads:**
- **In-process cache** with a short TTL (1-5 seconds) in every app server. A key read 50,000 times per second becomes one cache read per server per TTL.
- **Replicate the key** across cache nodes (for example `post:42#0..#7`) and pick a replica at random on read.
- **Request coalescing** (singleflight): concurrent misses for the same key wait for one backend fetch.
- **CDN** for public content.

**Hot writes:**
- **Split the counter**: write `likes:42:{random 0..15}` and sum the 16 sub-counters on read (or periodically into a cached total). Writes spread across shards; reads cost a little more.
- **Buffer and batch**: accumulate increments in memory or a log and apply them every second.
- **Avoid monotonic partition keys**: partition by hash of id rather than timestamp, or prefix time-based keys with a bucket number.
- For contended inventory, move to a single owner process per item that serialises updates, or pre-split stock into buckets.

**Detection**: track request rate per key at the cache layer (sampled top-k, for example with a count-min sketch), alert on keys above a threshold, and let the application promote detected keys to the local cache automatically. Redis offers `--hotkeys` analysis with LFU policies; managed stores like DynamoDB expose contributor insights.

**Consistent hashing** distributes many keys evenly and limits reshuffling when nodes change, but it does nothing for one key with disproportionate traffic. That distinction is exactly what the interviewer is checking.

**Trade-offs to state:** local caches add staleness (a takedown or edit takes up to the TTL to propagate; mitigate with invalidation broadcasts); split counters make reads more expensive and totals slightly delayed.
followUps: How do you detect hot keys in production?
What does key splitting do to reads?
How does consistent hashing help or not help?
mistakes: Weak answers assume consistent hashing spreads a single hot key.
Weak answers add more shards, which does not help one key.
Weak answers forget the write side: counters and likes on viral items.
Weak answers have no detection or monitoring story.

questions.q: Design a URL shortener like bit.ly.
questions.answer:
**It is a read-heavy key-value service: create a mapping from a 7-character base62 code to a long URL, and resolve codes with a redirect served mostly from cache. The interesting parts are generating codes without collisions, keeping the redirect path fast, and recording analytics asynchronously.**

**Requirements**: create links (optional alias and expiry), redirect, per-link click stats. Redirect p99 around 50 ms at the server, highly available, codes never collide.

**Estimates** (100M new links a month, 100:1 reads to writes): about 40 creates/s and 4,000 redirects/s on average, 10-20k peak; 6 billion links over 5 years at about 500 bytes is about 3 TB. Base62 with 7 characters gives about 3.5 trillion codes, so 7 characters is plenty.

**API**: `POST /v1/links {url, alias?, expiresAt?}` with an `Idempotency-Key`; `GET /{code}` returns 302 with `Location`; `GET /v1/links/{code}/stats`.

**Data**: `links(code PK, long_url, owner_id, created_at, expires_at)`, partitioned by hash of code. Click events go to a log, aggregated into `(code, day) -> count`.

```text
 client -> LB -> redirect service -> in-proc LRU -> Redis -> DB replica
                     |
                     +--> click log (Kafka) -> aggregator -> rollups
 client -> API -> link service -> range allocator -> DB primary
```

**Code generation** (the main deep dive): a counter encoded in base62 never collides; to avoid a bottleneck, each server leases a block of ids (say 10,000) from a database sequence or Redis `INCRBY` and mints locally. To make codes non-sequential, pass the id through a reversible permutation before encoding. Alternatives: random codes with a unique constraint and retry (about 0.2% conflict rate when 6 billion of 3.5 trillion are used), or a truncated hash with collision handling.

**Redirect path**: in-process cache for viral keys, Redis cache-aside with negative caching of unknown codes, replicas behind it. Respond 302 so clicks keep reaching us for analytics (301 would be cached by browsers indefinitely).

**Analytics**: buffer click events and send them to a log; never write a counter row per click on the hot path.

**Failure and abuse**: the redirect service is stateless; if the allocator is down, servers keep minting from their leases; rate-limit creation per key and IP, check URLs against a malware list, and support takedown (410 plus cache purge).
followUps: How would you stop people enumerating all links?
What happens when one link goes viral?
How do you expire links?
How would you make redirects fast worldwide?
mistakes: Weak answers hash the URL and ignore collisions.
Weak answers use a single global counter with no plan for it failing.
Weak answers write analytics synchronously on the redirect path.
Weak answers never discuss 301 versus 302.

questions.q: How do you generate short codes without collisions at scale?
questions.answer:
**I prefer a counter encoded in base62 with ranges leased to each server: unique by construction, no lookup per write, and coordination only once per block of ids. If codes must not be guessable, I pass the id through a reversible permutation before encoding. Random codes with a unique constraint are a fine simpler alternative.**

**Option 1: leased counter ranges.**

```ts
// allocator: one atomic call per 10,000 ids
const end = await redis.incrby("link:id", 10_000);   // or a DB sequence with INCREMENT 10000
let next = end - 10_000;
function nextCode(): string {
  if (next >= end) throw new Error("lease exhausted, fetch another");
  return toBase62(permute(BigInt(next++)));            // permute = keyed bijection
}
```

Properties: no collisions ever; creates need no uniqueness read; a crashed server wastes the remainder of its block, which is irrelevant in a 3.5 trillion code space; if the allocator is briefly unavailable, servers keep minting from their current block. Twitter's Snowflake applies a related idea to general ids: timestamp bits, worker id bits and a per-worker sequence give unique, roughly time-sorted 64-bit ids with no per-id coordination.

**Option 2: random codes.** Seven random base62 characters from a CSPRNG, inserted with a primary-key constraint; on conflict, generate again. With 6 billion codes used out of 3.5 trillion, about 1 in 580 inserts conflicts, so retries are cheap. Not enumerable by design. The uniqueness must be enforced by the database constraint (insert and catch the error), not by "check then insert", which races.

**Option 3: hash the URL.** Take the first 7 base62 characters of a SHA-256 of the URL. Deterministic (same URL, same code), but truncation guarantees collisions at billions of links by the birthday bound, so you still need detect-and-rehash. Also, different users shortening the same URL share a code, which mixes their analytics.

**Comparison:**

| | Collisions | Write cost | Guessable | Coordination |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Leased counter | None | Insert only | Yes, unless permuted | Per block |
| Random | Rare, retry | Insert + possible retry | No | None |
| Truncated hash | Certain at scale | Insert + retry | No | None |

**Permutation detail**: a small Feistel network or multiplication by an odd constant modulo 62^7 maps ids to codes one-to-one, so uniqueness is kept and consecutive ids look unrelated. It is obfuscation, not security; if links are truly private, require auth on the target.

**Custom aliases** share the table and constraint. Keep generated codes at exactly 7 characters and require aliases to differ (longer, or containing a hyphen), plus a reserved-word list (`api`, `login`).
followUps: What exactly happens if a server crashes mid-range?
How does Snowflake generate ids without coordination?
How do you make sure custom aliases never collide with generated codes?
mistakes: Weak answers truncate a hash and assume collisions will not happen.
Weak answers check uniqueness with a read followed by a write, which races.
Weak answers make every create call a central counter.
Weak answers produce sequential, enumerable codes for private links.

questions.q: Should a URL shortener return 301 or 302, and why does it matter?
questions.answer:
**I default to 302 (or 307). A 301 is permanent, so browsers may cache it indefinitely and stop contacting the shortener, which means repeat clicks are invisible to analytics and the link cannot be changed or taken down for those clients. A 302 sends every click through the service, at the cost of more traffic.**

**What each status means:**
- **301 Moved Permanently**: clients and caches may store the redirect and reuse it without asking again. Some clients historically changed POST to GET on 301.
- **302 Found**: temporary; not cached unless headers say so. Historically clients also changed POST to GET.
- **307 Temporary Redirect / 308 Permanent Redirect**: like 302/301 but guarantee the method and body are preserved. For GET-only redirects, 302 and 307 behave the same.

**Why the choice matters for a shortener:**

| Concern | 301 | 302/307 |
|---|---|---|
| Server load | Lower after first visit | Every click hits you |
| Latency for repeat visits | Fastest (no request) | One extra round trip |
| Click analytics | Undercounted | Accurate |
| Editing destination | Stale for cached clients | Immediate |
| Takedown of malicious links | Impossible for cached clients | Immediate |

Bitly-style products that sell analytics use non-permanent redirects for exactly this reason.

**Middle ground**: 302 with `Cache-Control: private, max-age=300` lets a browser reuse the redirect for five minutes, cutting repeat traffic while keeping links editable on a short horizon. At a CDN, a short `s-maxage` on 302 responses lets the edge serve redirects, and clicks are counted from CDN logs instead of origin.

**SEO** is sometimes raised: search engines treat 301 as passing ranking signals to the target. For a shortener that is rarely the goal; for a site migration (old URL to new URL forever), 301 or 308 is correct.

**In an interview** this question is really "do you connect protocol semantics to product requirements?". Name the requirement (analytics, editability, abuse takedown), pick the status, and state the cost.
followUps: What is the difference between 302 and 307?
Can you cache a 302 at a CDN and still count clicks?
How does the redirect choice affect link takedown?
mistakes: Weak answers say 301 is better for SEO and stop there.
Weak answers do not connect caching behaviour to analytics.
Weak answers forget that a cached 301 cannot be revoked for that client.
Weak answers confuse 302 and 307 semantics for non-GET methods.

questions.q: Design the home timeline for a Twitter-like service.
questions.answer:
**I precompute timelines with fan-out on write for most authors, stored as capped lists of post ids in a sharded Redis, and pull posts from very high-follower accounts at read time. A timeline read merges the two, hydrates ids from post and user caches, filters, and returns a cursor page.**

**Scope**: post, follow, home timeline (reverse chronological to start), user timeline. Feed loads p99 under about 200 ms; new posts visible to followers within seconds.

**Estimates** (300M DAU, 5 feed loads a day, 20% post daily, 200 followers average): about 15k feed reads/s average and 45k peak; about 600 posts/s; about 120k timeline inserts/s from fan-out. Keeping 800 ids of 8 bytes per active user is about 6.4 KB each, around 2 TB raw for 300M users, so a sharded in-memory cluster limited to active users.

**Data**: posts with time-sortable 64-bit ids (Snowflake-style) so sorting by id is sorting by time; follows stored in both directions; `home_tl:{user}` as a Redis list or sorted set capped at about 800 ids; post, user and counter caches for hydration.

```text
 post -> post service -> posts DB -> event (Kafka) -> fan-out workers
                                                        | follower lists (graph service)
                                                        v
                                           home timeline cache (Redis, by user)
 read -> timeline service: cached ids + pulled celebrity posts -> merge
          -> hydrate (multi-get post/user/counters) -> filter -> page + cursor
```

**Write path**: persist the post, update the author's own timeline synchronously (read-your-own-writes), publish an event; workers page through followers and `LPUSH` + `LTRIM` the id. Skip followers inactive for 30+ days; they get a pull-based rebuild when they return.

**Celebrities**: authors above a threshold (for example 1M followers) are not fanned out. At read time, the service fetches their recent posts from a hot per-author cache and merges by id.

**Edge cases**: deletes are filtered at hydration (the post cache returns tombstones) rather than removed from every list; unfollows are filtered against the current follow set; a new follow backfills a few recent posts asynchronously; a lost cache shard is rebuilt by pulling.

**Failure**: during spikes, fan-out lag grows; the queue absorbs it and we can temporarily raise the celebrity threshold. Twitter's 2012 "Timelines at Scale" talk describes this architecture closely, including Redis-backed home timelines of about 800 entries.
followUps: How large is the timeline cache and what happens if you lose it?
How do you handle a user who follows 5,000 accounts?
How do new follows and unfollows show up?
mistakes: Weak answers pick pure fan-out on write without noticing celebrity accounts.
Weak answers store full tweet objects in every follower's timeline.
Weak answers forget the author must see their own post immediately.
Weak answers chase deleted posts through millions of timelines instead of filtering on read.

questions.q: Fan-out on write or fan-out on read: how do you choose, and what do you do about celebrities?
questions.answer:
**I choose based on the read/write ratio and the follower distribution. Most social products read far more than they write, so fan-out on write is the default, but a pure push model breaks on accounts with millions of followers. The standard answer is hybrid: push for normal accounts, pull for celebrities at read time, plus skipping inactive followers.**

**The trade-off:**

| | Fan-out on write (push) | Fan-out on read (pull) |
|---|---|---|
| Cost per post | O(followers) inserts | O(1) |
| Cost per read | O(1) list read | O(followees) fetches + merge |
| Freshness | Delayed by fan-out | Immediate |
| Wasted work | Pushing to people who never read | None |
| Breaks on | Celebrities | Users following thousands |

**Quantify the celebrity problem**: an account with 50 million followers posting under pure push generates 50 million cache inserts. Even if the fan-out fleet does a million inserts per second, that post takes most of a minute to propagate and starves other authors' fan-out. With several celebrities posting during a live event, lag compounds.

**Hybrid design:**
1. Mark authors above a threshold as pull-only. The threshold comes from capacity: pick it so fan-out jobs finish within the freshness SLO at peak. Hundreds of thousands to about a million followers is a common range.
2. On read, take the precomputed list and merge recent posts from the (few) celebrities the user follows. Users typically follow a handful of such accounts, so the merge is cheap.
3. Keep celebrity recent-post lists extremely hot: replicate them across cache nodes and hold them in-process with a short TTL, because every timeline read touches them. This is the hot-key cost you accepted by pulling.
4. Skip fan-out to inactive users; rebuild their timeline on demand.
5. Order fan-out work so small accounts are not stuck behind large ones (separate queues by follower count).

**The other extreme**: a user following 5,000 accounts is expensive in a pull model but cheap in push, which is another reason push is the default.

**Ranking** shifts the picture: the precomputed list becomes one candidate source among several (out-of-network recommendations, trending), and the ranker scores a few hundred to a few thousand candidates. Fan-out still matters because in-network candidates must be retrieved fast; pulling for celebrities fits naturally as another candidate source.

**Failure angle**: if fan-out lags badly, temporarily lowering the threshold (pull more authors) trades read cost for freshness, a useful operational lever to mention.
followUps: How would you pick the follower threshold?
What happens to the celebrity's recent-posts cache under load?
How does ranking change the trade-off?
mistakes: Weak answers treat the choice as all-or-nothing.
Weak answers do not quantify write amplification for large accounts.
Weak answers ignore wasted fan-out to inactive users.
Weak answers move the celebrity cost to reads without addressing the resulting hot key.

questions.q: How would you add ranking to a chronological feed?
questions.answer:
**Ranking turns the feed into a pipeline: generate a few hundred to a few thousand candidates from several sources, fetch features in bulk, score them with a cheap model and then a heavier one, apply filters and diversity rules, and serve a page. The precomputed chronological timeline becomes one candidate source rather than the answer.**

```text
candidate sources          features              scoring               post-processing
- in-network timeline  ->  author affinity   ->  light model prunes -> dedup, diversity
- celebrity pulls          post age, media       to ~hundreds          (no 5 posts from one
- out-of-network recs      engagement counts  ->  heavy model scores    author), integrity
- trending                 viewer history                              filters, ads mixing
```

**Candidate generation** must be cheap and high recall: the in-network timeline cache, recent posts from celebrities, and recommendation sources (embedding similarity, "people like you engaged with"). Twitter's 2023 open-sourced recommendation code describes this shape: candidate sources, a light ranker, a heavy neural ranker, then heuristics and filters.

**Features** are fetched in batch from feature stores: viewer-author interaction history, post engagement velocity, recency, content type, viewer's recent behaviour. Precompute expensive features offline; compute cheap real-time ones (age, current like count) at request time.

**Scoring** predicts the probability of actions (like, reply, share, dwell, hide) and combines them into a value score with weights the product chooses. A two-stage cascade keeps latency in budget: the heavy model sees only the top few hundred.

**Post-processing**: author and topic diversity, removing seen posts, integrity and policy filters, inserting ads or prompts. Keep some recency so the feed does not feel stale.

**Pagination**: scores change constantly, so cursor-by-score skips or repeats items. Common approach: rank a larger set once at session start, store the ordered ids briefly (in a session cache), and paginate over that snapshot; refresh on pull-to-refresh.

**Latency**: candidate retrieval in parallel, batched feature fetches, model serving on dedicated inference hosts, and a strict timeout with a fallback to chronological order if ranking fails. A degraded chronological feed is better than an error.

**Evaluation**: offline metrics first, then A/B tests on engagement, retention and negative signals (hides, unfollows, reports). Optimising only for clicks tends to reward outrage, which is why mature teams include negative feedback and long-term retention in the objective.
followUps: How do you paginate a ranked feed when scores change?
How do you keep ranking latency under budget?
How would you evaluate a new ranking model safely?
mistakes: Weak answers say 'use machine learning' without a pipeline.
Weak answers score every possible post instead of generating candidates first.
Weak answers ignore pagination consistency for ranked results.
Weak answers forget filtering, diversity and integrity rules after scoring.

questions.q: Design a chat system like WhatsApp or Slack.
questions.answer:
**Clients keep a WebSocket to a fleet of gateway servers. A chat service that owns each conversation dedups, assigns a per-conversation sequence number, persists to a store partitioned by conversation, and delivers through a session registry that maps users to gateways, falling back to push notifications for offline devices.**

**Scope**: 1:1 and group chat, history across devices, delivery and read receipts, presence, offline push, media. Latency under about 300 ms when both are online; no loss after the server acknowledges.

**Estimates** (500M DAU, 40 messages each a day): about 200k messages/s average, 500k peak; about 4 TB a day of message data; around 150M concurrent sockets, which means hundreds to thousands of gateway servers depending on how many connections each holds.

```text
 device --WSS--> gateway --> chat service (owner of conversation, by consistent hash)
                                | dedup (sender, clientMsgId) -> assign seq -> persist
                                v
                       message store (partition: conversation_id + time bucket,
                                      clustering: seq)
                                |
                     members -> session registry (Redis: user -> gateway, device)
                        online: push via gateway      offline: APNs / FCM
```

**Send**: the device sends `{clientMsgId, conversationId, body}`; the owner dedups, assigns `seq`, writes durably, then acks `sent` with the seq (one tick). **Deliver**: look up members' sessions and push to their gateways; device acks become `delivered` receipts; read receipts carry `last_read_seq`.

**Storage**: a wide-column store fits append plus range-scan by conversation. Bucket partitions by time so old busy channels do not create huge partitions; Discord described this pattern for Cassandra and later ScyllaDB.

**Sync**: on reconnect a device sends its last seq per conversation and receives everything after it; long gaps page over HTTP.

**Groups**: store each message once per conversation and push to online members; for very large channels, gateways subscribe to channels so the owner publishes once per gateway rather than once per member (Slack's channel servers and gateway servers work roughly like this).

**Presence**: heartbeats into TTL keys, pushed only to users actively looking.

**Media**: presigned upload to object storage, message carries a reference, CDN serves downloads.

**Failure**: a gateway crash means clients reconnect elsewhere with jittered backoff; the registry TTL clears stale sessions; messages are already persisted. An owner crash moves ownership; the new owner reads the last seq before accepting writes.
followUps: How do you route a message to a user connected to another server?
How does a new device get its history?
How would you support a 100,000-member channel?
What changes with end-to-end encryption?
mistakes: Weak answers use HTTP polling without discussing persistent connections.
Weak answers acknowledge messages before they are durably stored.
Weak answers order messages by client timestamps.
Weak answers forget multi-device sync and offline push notifications.

questions.q: How do you guarantee message ordering and delivery receipts in a chat system?
questions.answer:
**Ordering only needs to hold within a conversation, so I give each conversation a single sequencer that assigns increasing sequence numbers after dedup and before acknowledging. Delivery is at-least-once with client-generated message ids for dedup, and receipts are watermarks: "delivered up to seq N" and "read up to seq N" per member.**

**Ordering:**
- The owner for a conversation (chosen by consistent hashing, or a single log partition keyed by conversation id) assigns `seq = last + 1` atomically and persists before acknowledging.
- Clients render by seq. Timestamps are for display, because phone clocks drift and two sends can share a millisecond.
- Gaps are detectable: a device holding seq 10 that receives 12 fetches 11.
- Failover needs fencing: the new owner takes a lease with a higher epoch, reads the last persisted seq, and the store rejects writes carrying an older epoch, so two owners cannot assign the same seq during a network split.

**Delivery protocol:**

```text
device A                      server (owner)                   device B
 send {clientMsgId=u1}  --->  dedup(A,u1)? no -> seq=42, persist
                        <---  sent {u1, seq=42}            ---> message {seq=42}
 (retry with u1 on timeout;                                 <--- ack {seq=42}
  server returns seq=42 again)  receipt delivered upTo 42 --->
                                                            <--- read {upTo=42}
                        <---  receipt read upTo 42
```

- The sender keeps the message as pending and retries with the same `clientMsgId` until it gets `sent`. The server's dedup table `(sender, clientMsgId) -> seq` (with a TTL of days) makes retries idempotent.
- Recipients ignore a seq they already have, so redeliveries are invisible.
- Exactly-once delivery is not achievable over a network; at-least-once plus dedup on both ends gives exactly-once display.

**Receipts as watermarks**: per member per conversation, store `delivered_seq` and `last_read_seq`. Reading message 42 implies 1-41 are read. One small update per read action instead of a row per message per member, which matters in a 500-member group. "Read by 12" is a count of members whose `last_read_seq >= 42`, computed on demand or cached.

**Multi-device**: track watermarks per device for delivery and per user for read (reading on the laptop marks it read on the phone; the server syncs that watermark to the user's other devices).

**Edits and deletes** are new events in the same sequence referencing the original seq, so every device applies them in order.

**Trade-off to state**: a single owner per conversation limits throughput of one conversation to what one sequencer can do (thousands of messages per second is plenty for any chat), in exchange for simple total ordering.
followUps: What happens if two servers both think they own a conversation?
How do you show 'read by 12 people' efficiently in a group?
How do you handle an edit or delete?
mistakes: Weak answers rely on client or server wall-clock timestamps for order.
Weak answers promise exactly-once delivery without idempotency ids.
Weak answers store a receipt row per message per member in large groups.
Weak answers ignore failover of the sequencer.

questions.q: How do you implement online presence for millions of users?
questions.answer:
**Presence is derived from heartbeats: each gateway refreshes a short-TTL key per connected user, so a user without heartbeats simply expires to offline. Changes are pushed only to clients currently viewing that user, debounced to absorb flapping, and large groups show counts rather than per-member status.**

**Why it is hard**: presence changes constantly, and naive fan-out multiplies. If 100M users each have 200 contacts and change status 10 times a day, broadcasting every change is 200 billion updates a day, most to people who are not looking.

**Design:**

```text
 device --heartbeat 30s--> gateway --batch--> presence service
                                               | SET presence:{user} online EX 60
                                               | (TTL expiry = offline)
                                               v
                               subscribers: who is viewing user X right now?
                                   subscribe on opening chat list / conversation
                                   unsubscribe on leaving
                                               |
                                 push changes only to subscribers' gateways
```

- **Heartbeats with TTL**: the gateway knows which sockets are alive; it batches presence refreshes for all its users every 30 seconds. If a gateway dies, its users expire within a minute without anyone sending "offline".
- **Interest-based fan-out**: when a client opens a conversation list, it subscribes to presence for the visible contacts; the presence service keeps `user -> subscribers` and pushes changes only there.
- **Debounce**: wait 10-30 seconds before announcing offline, since mobile connections drop briefly all the time. Show "online" immediately but "offline" late.
- **Last seen**: write it on disconnect or every few minutes to a durable store, not on every heartbeat. Coarse granularity ("last seen today at 14:05") is fine and respects privacy settings that hide it.
- **Large groups**: showing live status for 50,000 members is pointless; show an online count (approximate, computed periodically) and live status only for the visible member list.

**Storage**: Redis (or an in-memory service sharded by user id) for current presence; small and rebuildable from heartbeats within a minute, so durability is unnecessary.

**Trade-offs**: shorter TTLs give fresher presence but more heartbeat traffic and battery use; interest-based fan-out adds subscription bookkeeping but cuts traffic by orders of magnitude. Discord's and Slack's engineering posts both describe presence as one of the most expensive real-time features at their scale, which is why these optimisations matter.
followUps: How do you handle a phone that flaps between online and offline every few seconds?
How would presence work in a 50,000-member server?
Where would you store last-seen and how often do you write it?
mistakes: Weak answers broadcast every status change to all contacts.
Weak answers rely only on explicit disconnect events, which never arrive when a phone loses signal.
Weak answers write presence to the primary database on every heartbeat.
Weak answers ignore privacy settings for last seen.

questions.q: Design the driver matching system for a ride-hailing app like Uber.
questions.answer:
**Drivers stream locations into an in-memory geospatial index partitioned by region. When a rider requests a trip, the dispatcher pulls nearby available drivers, ranks them by road-network ETA, and offers the trip to the best one through an atomic compare-and-set on the driver's state with an expiry, moving to the next candidate on decline or timeout. Trips live in a strongly consistent store as a state machine.**

**Scale**: 5M online drivers updating every 4 seconds is about 1.25M location writes per second, but the live index is only around 1 GB. Trip requests are hundreds per second globally, so matching can afford real computation per request.

```text
 driver app --stream--> location service --> geo index (H3/geohash cells, in memory, by city)
                                     \--> Kafka (history, ETA training, surge)
 rider --> trip service (trip: requested) --> dispatcher (owns a region)
             1. candidates: rider cell + k-ring, available, right vehicle type
             2. prune to ~20 by distance, ETA from routing service (road graph + traffic)
             3. CAS driver_state available -> offered(trip, expires 15s)
             4. push offer; accept -> trip driver_assigned, driver on_trip
                decline/timeout -> release driver, next candidate
```

**Ranking**: straight-line distance is misleading (rivers, highways, one-way streets). ETA on the road graph is the real metric, plus driver acceptance likelihood, rating and vehicle fit. ETA is expensive, so compute it only for the top candidates.

**Atomic assignment**: the geo index is eventually consistent and may be seconds stale, but assignment must be exact. `UPDATE driver_state SET status='offered', trip_id=?, version=version+1 WHERE driver_id=? AND status='available' AND version=?`. Zero rows updated means someone else took the driver. Making one dispatcher partition own each region reduces contention to borders, where the CAS still protects correctness.

**Offers**: carry an expiry. If the dispatcher crashes, the offer expires, a sweeper returns the driver to available, and the trip goes back to matching. Accepting checks the offer is still valid.

**Batching**: greedy first-come matching can be globally poor (assigning the only nearby driver to rider A when rider B is even closer to them). Collecting requests over a one- to two-second window per region and solving an assignment problem (minimise total pickup time) improves dense-city outcomes at the cost of a small delay.

**Trip state machine**: requested -> matching -> driver_assigned -> arrived -> in_progress -> completed -> paid, with cancellations; transitions are conditional updates and each emits an event.

**Reliability**: the location index rebuilds itself within one update interval after a crash; trips and driver state are replicated and durable; trip creation is idempotent so a double tap does not create two trips.
followUps: Why not just pick the geographically nearest driver?
How would batching requests improve matches?
What happens if the dispatcher crashes after sending an offer?
How do you partition by city and handle borders?
mistakes: Weak answers rank drivers by straight-line distance only.
Weak answers have no atomic assignment, allowing one driver to get two trips.
Weak answers persist every location update synchronously to a durable database.
Weak answers ignore offer timeouts and declines.

questions.q: How would you index millions of moving driver locations for nearby search?
questions.answer:
**I map each location to a cell id (geohash, H3 or S2) and keep an in-memory index from cell to the set of drivers in it, partitioned by city. A nearby query looks up the rider's cell plus its neighbours, expands the ring until it has enough candidates, then filters by exact distance and availability.**

**Why cells**: a spatial index turns a 2D range query into a handful of key lookups. Without it, "drivers within 2 km" scans every driver.

**Write path** (about 1.25M updates/s at 5M drivers every 4 seconds):

```python
def on_update(driver_id, lat, lng):
    cell = h3.latlng_to_cell(lat, lng, 9)
    prev = state.get(driver_id)
    if prev is None or prev.cell != cell:          # most updates stay in the same cell
        if prev: index[prev.cell].discard(driver_id)
        index[cell].add(driver_id)
    state[driver_id] = Loc(lat, lng, cell, now())
```

Most updates do not cross a cell boundary, so they only overwrite the driver's position. History goes asynchronously to Kafka and cheap storage.

**Read path**: `cells = grid_disk(rider_cell, k)` with k = 1, and grow k until at least N available drivers are found or a maximum radius is hit. Then compute haversine distances, filter by status and vehicle, and hand the top candidates to ETA ranking.

**Choice of index:**

| Index | Notes |
|---|---|
| Geohash | Base32 prefix strings; precision 6 is about 1.2 x 0.6 km. Simple, Redis `GEOADD`/`GEOSEARCH` support. Boundary and polar distortion issues. |
| H3 | Hexagons at 16 resolutions; all six neighbours equidistant, so rings are uniform. Built by Uber for marketplace analytics. |
| S2 | Hilbert-curve cells on a cube projection; exact hierarchy and good range-scan locality. |
| Quadtree | Adapts to density by splitting crowded cells; more churn with moving points. |

**Density**: a fixed resolution gives hundreds of drivers per cell downtown and none in the countryside. Expanding rings handle sparse areas; for dense areas pick a finer resolution or cap results per cell.

**Storage choice**: Redis GEO sets sharded by city are a fine interview answer for simplicity (`GEOSEARCH key FROMLONLAT lng lat BYRADIUS 2 km ASC COUNT 50`). A custom in-memory service per region gives more control (H3 cells, vehicle filters) at higher build cost.

**Durability**: none needed for the live index. If a node dies, drivers re-report within seconds and the index rebuilds, which is why keeping it in memory is safe.

**Stale data**: entries older than about 15-30 seconds are treated as offline and evicted, so a driver whose app died does not get offers.
followUps: How do you handle very dense and very sparse areas?
How do you move a driver between cells efficiently?
When would you use a quadtree instead?
mistakes: Weak answers run distance calculations over a relational table for every query.
Weak answers forget to search neighbouring cells.
Weak answers write every location update to a durable database synchronously.
Weak answers choose one fixed radius regardless of density.

questions.q: What is a geohash and what are its edge cases?
questions.answer:
**A geohash encodes latitude and longitude into a short base32 string by interleaving their bits, so each extra character narrows the area and points that share a prefix are in the same cell. Its main edge case is that nearby points can straddle a cell boundary and share no prefix, so searches must include neighbouring cells.**

**How it works**: repeatedly halve the longitude range and the latitude range, alternating, writing 1 for the upper half and 0 for the lower; group bits into 5s and encode in base32. Approximate cell sizes:

```text
length  cell size (approx)
  4     39 km x 20 km
  5     4.9 km x 4.9 km
  6     1.2 km x 0.61 km
  7     153 m x 153 m
  8     38 m x 19 m
```

Because it is a string, a prefix query (`WHERE geohash LIKE 'u4pru%'` or a sorted-set range) finds everything in a cell, which works with ordinary indexes and key-value stores.

**Edge cases:**
1. **Boundaries**: two points a metre apart on either side of a cell edge have different hashes; at the equator or prime meridian even the first character differs. Fix: query the cell and its 8 neighbours, then filter by real distance.
2. **Shape and distortion**: cells are rectangles in degrees; they get narrower east-west towards the poles, so a "1 km" precision is not 1 km everywhere.
3. **Precision vs radius**: a cell is not a circle. Pick the precision whose cell is about the search radius, search the 3 x 3 block, and post-filter with haversine distance.
4. **Density**: one precision gives too many points downtown and too few in rural areas; expand to coarser cells or more rings when results are sparse.
5. **Z-order jumps**: the curve is not perfectly local; adjacent cells can be far apart in sort order, which is another reason to query neighbours explicitly.

**In practice**: Redis GEO commands store members in a sorted set with a 52-bit geohash-based score and handle neighbour search for you via `GEOSEARCH`. For analytics like surge pricing, H3 hexagons are often preferred because every neighbour is the same distance from the centre, which makes smoothing over neighbouring cells uniform.
followUps: How do you choose the precision for a 1 km search?
How does Redis store geo data?
Why would you prefer H3 for surge pricing?
mistakes: Weak answers assume nearby points always share a prefix.
Weak answers search only the single cell containing the query point.
Weak answers ignore that cell width shrinks towards the poles.
Weak answers confuse geohash precision with an exact radius.

questions.q: Design a video streaming platform like YouTube or Netflix.
questions.answer:
**Uploads go directly to object storage through resumable presigned uploads; a workflow splits each video into chunks and transcodes them in parallel into a bitrate ladder, packaged as HLS/DASH segments; players fetch segments over HTTP from a CDN and switch quality per segment. Metadata, views and watch state are ordinary services beside that.**

**Clarify first**: YouTube means huge upload volume (it has cited more than 500 hours uploaded per minute) and a long tail; Netflix means a smaller catalogue encoded very carefully and pre-positioned near viewers.

**Estimates**: hundreds of terabytes of originals per day for a YouTube-like product, and egress in the tens to hundreds of terabits per second at peak. Conclusion: delivery must come from CDN edges or ISP-embedded caches, and transcoding must be massively parallel.

```text
 creator -> presigned resumable upload -> object storage (originals)
              upload_complete event -> workflow (DAG)
                 validate -> split by GOP -> encode chunk x rendition x codec (parallel)
                 -> package CMAF (HLS + DASH manifests) -> publish, status=ready
 viewer -> CDN edge -> shield -> origin storage
 viewer -> API: metadata, manifest URL, signed token, watch position, view events -> Kafka
```

**Upload**: chunked and resumable (8-16 MB parts) so multi-gigabyte uploads survive mobile networks; idempotent completion handler.

**Transcoding**: split at keyframes into chunks, encode each chunk for each rendition and codec in parallel, stitch, cut delivery segments of a few seconds, write manifests. Retries are per task; outputs go to deterministic paths. Encode a fast H.264 ladder first so the video is watchable quickly; add expensive codecs (VP9, AV1) for videos that get popular. Netflix's per-title encoding chooses a ladder per title from quality measurements.

**Playback**: the master playlist lists renditions; the player measures throughput and buffer and picks the rendition for each next segment (hls.js, dash.js or Shaka Player on Media Source Extensions in browsers).

**Delivery**: edge caching of immutable segments, an origin shield to collapse misses, multi-CDN failover, signed URLs and DRM for premium content. Netflix's Open Connect appliances inside ISPs serve most of its traffic and are filled off-peak.

**Metadata and counts**: sharded relational store for video metadata; view events batched through Kafka into aggregated counters with bot filtering; watch position upserted every few seconds.

**Failure**: worker death retries one task; keep originals so you can re-encode after a bad encoder release; CDN failure triggers switching to an alternate host.
followUps: How do you make a new upload playable within minutes?
How does the player choose quality?
How would you reduce CDN costs?
What changes for live streaming?
mistakes: Weak answers send video bytes through API servers or store them in a database.
Weak answers transcode sequentially on one machine.
Weak answers treat the CDN as optional.
Weak answers do not distinguish YouTube's long tail from Netflix's curated catalogue.

questions.q: How does adaptive bitrate streaming work end to end?
questions.answer:
**The video is encoded at several bitrates and resolutions and each version is cut into short, aligned segments listed in a manifest. The player downloads the manifest, then fetches segments one by one over plain HTTP, choosing the quality of each next segment from measured throughput and how full its buffer is.**

**End to end:**
1. **Encode a ladder**: for example 240p at a few hundred kbps up to 1080p at a few Mbps (and 4K higher), possibly in several codecs.
2. **Segment**: cut every rendition into segments of a few seconds (Apple's HLS guidance targets about 6 seconds) with keyframes at the same timestamps, so switching between renditions at a boundary is seamless.
3. **Manifest**: HLS uses `.m3u8` playlists (a master playlist listing renditions with `BANDWIDTH` and `RESOLUTION`, and a media playlist per rendition listing segments); DASH uses an XML `.mpd`. CMAF lets both reference the same fMP4 segments.
4. **Deliver**: segments are immutable files with stable URLs, so CDNs cache them like any static asset.
5. **Play**: the player fetches the master playlist, starts with a conservative rendition for a fast start, measures how long each segment took to download, and adjusts.

```text
time ->   seg1   seg2   seg3   seg4   seg5
quality:  480p   720p   1080p  720p   720p
          start  network good  bandwidth dropped, buffer protecting
```

**ABR algorithms**: throughput-based (estimate bandwidth from recent downloads, pick the highest rendition below it with a safety margin), buffer-based (pick quality from buffer level; BOLA, used in dash.js, is an example), or hybrids. The goal is to balance quality, rebuffering (the worst experience) and switching frequency.

**In browsers**, JavaScript players (hls.js, dash.js, Shaka) download segments with `fetch` and append them to a `SourceBuffer` via Media Source Extensions. Safari also plays HLS natively.

**Segment length trade-off**: shorter segments adapt faster and reduce live latency but mean more requests and slightly worse compression; longer segments are more efficient but react slowly.

**Live**: playlists are updated continuously as segments are produced; latency is roughly segment duration times the number of segments buffered. Low-latency HLS and DASH use partial segments and preload hints to reach a few seconds.

**HLS vs DASH**: HLS is Apple's protocol (RFC 8216) and required for native Apple playback; DASH is an MPEG standard, codec-agnostic. Most platforms produce both from one set of CMAF segments.
followUps: What is the difference between HLS and DASH?
Why are segments usually a few seconds long?
How does low-latency live streaming change this?
mistakes: Weak answers think the server decides the bitrate per viewer.
Weak answers forget that renditions must have aligned segment boundaries.
Weak answers do not mention the manifest/playlist.
Weak answers confuse progressive download with ABR.

questions.q: How would you design the transcoding pipeline for 500 hours of uploads per minute?
questions.answer:
**I run it as a DAG workflow: validate, split each upload into keyframe-aligned chunks, fan out encode tasks per chunk, rendition and codec to an autoscaled worker fleet, then stitch, package and publish. Tasks are idempotent with deterministic outputs, work is prioritised by expected popularity, and expensive codecs are applied lazily only to videos that earn it.**

**Scale**: 500 hours per minute is 30,000 hours of video every hour. Modern codecs encode much slower than real time per core, so this needs a very large fleet or hardware encoders, which is why work avoidance (not encoding what nobody watches in expensive formats) matters as much as parallelism.

```text
upload_complete
   -> inspect (codec, resolution, duration, corruption)  -> content safety scan
   -> split into N chunks at GOP boundaries (e.g. 10-30 s)
   -> fan-out: N chunks x R renditions x C codecs  (independent tasks on a queue)
   -> per rendition: concat chunks -> segment (2-6 s) -> manifests (HLS/DASH, CMAF)
   -> thumbnails, preview sprites, captions (parallel branch)
   -> publish: write to origin, mark ready, notify creator
```

**Orchestration**: a workflow engine (Temporal, Step Functions, or in-house like Netflix's Cosmos) tracks the DAG, retries failed tasks with backoff, and records progress so a crash resumes rather than restarts. Each task reads from object storage and writes to a path derived from `(video, rendition, chunk, encoder_version)`, so a retry overwrites identical output.

**Tiered encoding:**
1. **Fast path**: low-cost H.264 renditions up to 720p or 1080p, so the video is playable within minutes.
2. **Full ladder** at normal priority.
3. **Premium codecs** (VP9, AV1) and per-title optimisation only once a video crosses a view threshold, since bandwidth savings only pay off at volume.

**Prioritisation and backpressure**: separate queues for creators with large audiences, new uploads, and backfill/re-encode jobs; backfill uses spare capacity (spot instances). If queues grow, the fast path keeps priority so the user-visible "processing" time stays bounded.

**Chunk boundaries**: encode with closed GOPs and a fixed keyframe interval so chunks concatenate cleanly and segments align across renditions; otherwise ABR switching glitches.

**Quality control**: compute objective quality (for example VMAF, Netflix's metric) on samples; reject outputs below thresholds.

**Encoder rollout**: canary a new version on a small percentage of uploads, compare quality and failure rates, keep originals so any bad output can be re-encoded.

**Hardware**: GPUs or dedicated video ASICs give large throughput gains for common codecs; software encoders often reach better compression for premium encodes. Mixed fleets are common; YouTube has publicly described building its own video transcoding chips.
followUps: How do you prioritise uploads when the fleet is saturated?
How do you roll out a new encoder version safely?
Would you use GPUs or hardware encoders?
mistakes: Weak answers encode whole files on one worker.
Weak answers do not make tasks idempotent, so retries corrupt output.
Weak answers use the same expensive codec settings for every upload regardless of popularity.
Weak answers have no prioritisation or backpressure.

questions.q: Design a payment system like Stripe.
questions.answer:
**The core is a strongly consistent relational store holding payments as explicit state machines, a double-entry immutable ledger written in the same transaction as each state change, idempotency keys on every mutating API call, adapters to processors that treat timeouts as unknown outcomes, an outbox for events and webhooks, and daily reconciliation.**

**Scope**: create and capture payments, refunds, merchant payouts, webhooks, balances. Volume is modest (10M payments a day is about 100/s average, 1,000/s peak), so correctness dominates.

```text
 merchant -> API (auth, rate limit) -> payment service
   1. idempotency key claim (merchant, key, request hash)
   2. payment row: created -> risk check
   3. PSP adapter (idempotent reference) -> card network
   4. one DB transaction: state transition + ledger entries + outbox event + key response
 outbox relay -> Kafka -> webhook sender (signed, retried) -> merchant
 PSP webhooks -> verify signature, dedup event id -> conditional state transition
 nightly: settlement files -> reconciliation -> mismatches to ops
```

**Idempotency**: the key is stored with the request hash and the final response; a retry replays the response, a reused key with different parameters is rejected. Stripe documents this behaviour and notes keys can be pruned after 24 hours.

**State machine**: created, requires_action, processing, authorised, captured, refunded, failed, plus `unknown` for timeouts. Transitions are conditional updates on status and version, each writing a `payment_events` row.

**Ledger**: every transaction is a set of entries with debits equal to credits (capture: debit processor receivable, credit merchant payable and fee revenue). Entries are immutable; corrections are reversing entries. Balances are sums of entries, cached as running balances.

**Processors**: on timeout, do not mark failed and do not retry with a new id. Mark unknown and resolve by querying the processor with your reference or waiting for its webhook.

**Events**: the transactional outbox avoids the dual-write problem; consumers and merchants dedup by event id.

**Reconciliation**: match every ledger entry against processor and bank reports daily; mismatches are investigated. This catches the failure cases your design missed.

**Scale and regions**: shard by merchant so a payment and its entries stay on one shard; home each merchant in one region or use a consensus-replicated database. Avoid multi-master with last-writer-wins for money. Tokenise card data at the edge to shrink PCI scope.
followUps: What if the service crashes after the card was charged but before the result was saved?
How do you deliver webhooks reliably to merchants?
How would you go multi-region?
How do you compute a merchant's balance?
mistakes: Weak answers optimise for throughput and choose eventual consistency for money.
Weak answers retry timed-out charges without an idempotent reference.
Weak answers keep a mutable balance column as the source of truth.
Weak answers forget reconciliation against processor settlement files.

questions.q: How do idempotency keys work, and how would you implement them?
questions.answer:
**The client generates a unique key per logical operation and sends it with the request. The server atomically claims the key, performs the operation, and stores the response against the key; any retry with the same key gets the stored response instead of a second execution. Stripe popularised this with its `Idempotency-Key` header.**

**Table:**

```sql
CREATE TABLE idempotency_keys (
  merchant_id   text        NOT NULL,
  key           text        NOT NULL,
  request_hash  text        NOT NULL,
  status        text        NOT NULL,          -- in_progress | done
  response_code int,
  response_body jsonb,
  locked_until  timestamptz,
  created_at    timestamptz NOT NULL DEFAULT now(),
  PRIMARY KEY (merchant_id, key)
);
```

**Flow:**
1. `INSERT ... ON CONFLICT DO NOTHING RETURNING *` to claim the key atomically. If the insert wins, proceed.
2. If it conflicts, load the row:
   - `request_hash` differs: return an error (key reused with different parameters).
   - `status = done`: return the stored status code and body.
   - `status = in_progress` and lock not expired: return 409 so the client retries later.
   - lock expired: the previous worker died; take over carefully (see below).
3. Do the work. Pass a derived idempotent reference to downstream processors so your own retries to them are safe.
4. In the same transaction as the business state change, set `status = done` and store the response.

**Crash recovery**: if a worker crashes after calling the processor but before saving, a retry must not blindly re-charge. Brandur Leach's write-up on Stripe-style keys in Postgres models a request as phases with recovery points: the key row records which phase completed, so a retry resumes (for example, by querying the processor for the result of the reference) instead of starting over.

**What to cache**: final results, including deterministic errors like a card decline (the retry should get the same decline). Do not cache errors caused by your own transient failure before any side effect happened, or the client can never succeed; release the key instead.

**Retention**: long enough to cover realistic retries. Stripe says keys can be removed once they are at least 24 hours old. Use a TTL job or partitioned table to drop old rows.

**Scope**: keys are per merchant or per API key, never global, so two merchants' UUIDs never interact.

**Client guidance**: generate a fresh key per logical operation (not per HTTP attempt), retry with exponential backoff and jitter, and reuse the same key for all attempts of that operation.
followUps: What do you return if the first request is still in progress?
Should you cache a 500 error response for a key?
How long should keys be retained?
mistakes: Weak answers store the key but not the response, so retries cannot return the original result.
Weak answers check and insert the key non-atomically, allowing two concurrent requests through.
Weak answers ignore requests that reuse a key with different parameters.
Weak answers forget to pass an idempotent reference to downstream processors.

questions.q: Why do payment systems use double-entry ledgers?
questions.answer:
**Because every movement of money is recorded as entries on at least two accounts whose debits and credits sum to zero, money cannot appear or disappear without a matching record. Entries are immutable and balances are derived from them, so the system is auditable, self-checking and reconstructible at any point in time.**

**The model:**
- **Accounts**: merchant payable, platform fee revenue, processor receivable, bank cash, customer refunds payable, and so on, each with a currency.
- **Transactions**: a business event (capture, refund, payout).
- **Entries**: lines in a transaction, each a debit or credit to one account. Invariant per transaction: `sum(debits) = sum(credits)`.

```text
Capture 100.00, fee 3.00
  debit  processor_receivable   100.00
  credit merchant_payable        97.00
  credit fee_revenue              3.00
Refund 40.00 (fee kept)
  debit  merchant_payable        40.00
  credit processor_receivable    40.00
Payout 57.00
  debit  merchant_payable        57.00
  credit bank_cash               57.00
```

Merchant payable ends at 97 - 40 - 57 = 0: everything owed has been paid.

**Why not a balance column?**
- A balance that is wrong gives no clue why. With entries, you can find the exact transaction that caused a discrepancy.
- Concurrent updates to a balance invite lost updates; appending entries is simpler to reason about.
- Regulators and auditors need history; "balance = 97" is not history.
- Global invariant checks are trivial: the sum of all entries across all accounts must be zero.

**Rules:**
- **Immutable**: never update or delete an entry. Fix mistakes with a reversing transaction plus a correct one.
- **Integer minor units** (cents) and an explicit currency per account; never floats.
- **Atomicity**: the entries of a transaction are written in one database transaction with the business state change.
- **Fast balances**: maintain a running balance per account, updated in the same transaction (with a row lock or version check), and periodically verify it against the sum of entries.

**Real systems**: Square described building "Books", an immutable double-entry accounting service, for exactly these reasons; Modern Treasury's "accounting for developers" series is a readable primer. Double entry also makes reconciliation natural: each external report line should map to entries on the processor or bank accounts.
followUps: How do you correct a mistaken entry?
How do you get a balance quickly without summing millions of rows?
How would you represent a refund?
mistakes: Weak answers describe a ledger as a log of balance changes on one account.
Weak answers allow entries to be updated or deleted.
Weak answers use floating-point amounts.
Weak answers cannot explain what invariant double entry enforces.

questions.q: Can you get exactly-once processing in a distributed payment flow?
questions.answer:
**Not exactly-once delivery: across a network a sender cannot distinguish a lost request from a lost reply, so either it retries (risking duplicates) or it doesn't (risking loss). What you can build is exactly-once effect: at-least-once delivery combined with idempotent processing and deduplication at every hop, plus reconciliation to catch what still slips through.**

**The two generals view**: when a call to the card processor times out, the charge may or may not have happened. No protocol on your side removes that uncertainty; you must ask the other side or wait for its notification.

**How each hop gets exactly-once effect:**

| Hop | Mechanism |
|---|---|
| Client -> API | Idempotency key stored with response |
| API -> processor | Idempotent reference on the processor request; on timeout, mark `unknown` and query status |
| DB change -> events | Transactional outbox: write the event row in the same transaction; relay publishes; consumers dedup by event id |
| Consumer processing | Dedup table keyed by event id, updated in the same transaction as the side effect |
| Processor webhooks -> us | Verify signature, dedup by event id, apply as conditional state transitions |
| Us -> merchant webhooks | At-least-once with retries; merchants dedup by event id |

**Outbox detail:**

```text
BEGIN
  UPDATE payments SET status='captured', version=8 WHERE id=$1 AND version=7
  INSERT INTO ledger_entries ...
  INSERT INTO outbox (event_id, type, payload) VALUES (...)
COMMIT
relay: SELECT unpublished outbox rows -> publish to Kafka -> mark published
```

If the relay crashes after publishing but before marking, the event is published twice; consumers dedup. The point is that a committed state change can never be missing its event, and an event never exists for an uncommitted change.

**Kafka exactly-once semantics** (idempotent producers plus transactions) guarantee that a consume-transform-produce loop within Kafka does not duplicate or lose records. It does not extend to a call to a card network or a write to an external database unless that write participates in the same deduplication scheme.

**Out-of-order events**: a "succeeded" webhook can arrive before "processing". The state machine only applies valid forward transitions and ignores stale ones, keyed on status and version.

**Reconciliation** is the final safety net: compare the ledger with processor and bank settlement files, and route mismatches (charged but no record, recorded but not charged) to automated fixes or humans.

**Model answer in one sentence**: "Exactly-once is an illusion we construct from retries, idempotency keys, dedup tables and atomic outbox writes, and we verify it daily with reconciliation."
followUps: What does Kafka's exactly-once semantics actually cover?
How does the transactional outbox work?
How do you handle out-of-order webhooks?
mistakes: Weak answers claim a message broker gives end-to-end exactly-once including external calls.
Weak answers treat a timeout as a failure.
Weak answers publish events outside the database transaction (dual writes).
Weak answers have no reconciliation to catch what slips through.

questions.q: Design a search typeahead (autocomplete) service.
questions.answer:
**I serve suggestions from an in-memory prefix index (a trie or FST with the top-k completions precomputed at each node), built offline from aggregated, time-decayed query logs and shipped as immutable snapshots. A streaming job adds trending terms, and caching at the client, CDN and service layers keeps p99 latency within the keystroke budget.**

**Scope**: top 5-10 suggestions per prefix, refreshed daily plus trending within minutes to an hour, per locale, with policy filtering. Latency target about 50-100 ms end to end.

**Estimates**: 500M searches a day with about 6 requests per search after debouncing is about 30k QPS average, 90k peak. 100M candidate queries fit in memory as a compressed index on each server or across a few shards.

```text
 keystrokes -> debounce ~120 ms -> client cache -> CDN (short, non-personal prefixes)
            -> suggest service (in-memory index snapshot, LRU of hot prefixes)
            -> merge personal recent searches (separate small call or client-side)
 logs -> Kafka -> stream job (trending counts) ----------\
              \-> batch job (normalise, filter, decay, score) -> index builder
                     -> snapshot to object storage -> servers hot-swap
```

**Index**: walking `h-o-w` reaches the node for "how", which already stores its top-k suggestion ids and scores, so a lookup is O(prefix length). Memory is controlled with radix compression, suggestion ids instead of strings, or FSTs (Lucene's completion suggester uses them).

**Ranking**: decayed popularity, click-through, freshness boosts for trending terms, locale; personal recent searches merged on top. Normalise queries (case, Unicode, whitespace) before counting.

**Updates**: never mutate the serving structure per query; rebuild snapshots hourly or daily and overlay a small trending index.

**Sharding**: replicate the full index if it fits (simplest, no fan-out); otherwise shard by hash of the first few characters, not by first letter, to avoid hot shards.

**Client**: debounce, cancel stale requests with `AbortController`, ignore out-of-order responses, cache by prefix so backspace is instant.

**Safety**: blocklist applied at build time and again at serving time with hot reload; validate each snapshot before publishing and keep the previous one for instant rollback.

**Degradation**: on overload, return no suggestions; search itself must keep working.
followUps: How quickly can a trending query start appearing?
How do you personalise suggestions without breaking caching?
How do you keep offensive suggestions out?
mistakes: Weak answers update the serving data structure on every search.
Weak answers walk the whole subtree under a prefix at query time.
Weak answers ignore client-side debouncing and caching.
Weak answers forget content filtering and normalisation.

questions.q: Trie or inverted index for autocomplete: what are the trade-offs?
questions.answer:
**A trie or FST with precomputed top-k per node gives the lowest, most predictable latency for pure prefix completion with static popularity ranking. An inverted index with edge n-grams handles matching any word in the phrase, filters, fuzzy matching and dynamic scoring, at the cost of more memory and query-time work. Query suggestion on a search engine fits the first; product, people or document typeahead usually fits the second.**

**Trie / FST:**
- Lookup walks the prefix (O(length)) and returns the stored top-k list: microseconds.
- Matches only from the start of the indexed string: "pro" does not find "iphone pro" unless you also index every suffix or each word separately.
- Ranking is baked in at build time; per-request boosts or filters require extra structures.
- Updates mean rebuilding and swapping snapshots, which suits daily or hourly refreshes.
- FSTs share prefixes and suffixes and compress large key sets dramatically; Andrew Gallant's post on indexing 1.6 billion keys with FSTs is the classic explanation, and Lucene's completion suggester uses them.

**Inverted index with edge n-grams:**
- Each suggestion is tokenised; each token is indexed as its prefixes ("iph", "ipho", ...). A typed prefix becomes exact term lookups, then scoring.
- Matches any word, supports multi-word queries in any order, filters (category, in-stock, permissions), fuzzy matching with edit distance, and dynamic boosts (personalisation, recency).
- Index grows with n-gram expansion; queries do more work (posting list intersections, scoring).
- Near-real-time updates: a new product is suggestible within seconds.
- Elasticsearch's `search_as_you_type` field type builds these n-gram subfields for you.

| Need | Better fit |
|---|---|
| Pure prefix of popular queries, tight latency | Trie / FST |
| Infix / any-word match | Inverted index |
| Filters, permissions | Inverted index |
| Typo tolerance | Both possible (FST with Levenshtein automata; fuzzy queries) |
| Real-time additions | Inverted index |
| Smallest memory for huge key sets | FST |

**Running both** is common: a fast prefix index serves the top suggestions from popular queries, while an n-gram index supplies entity matches (products, people) and long-tail results, merged and deduplicated by the suggest service with a latency budget per source.

**Typo tolerance**: for a trie, walk with a bounded edit distance (expensive on large tries, efficient on FSTs via Levenshtein automata); for an inverted index, use fuzzy term queries, ideally only after the first two or three characters to keep candidate sets small.
followUps: How would you add typo tolerance to each approach?
How do edge n-grams affect index size?
When would you run both?
mistakes: Weak answers say tries are always faster without considering memory and features.
Weak answers miss that a plain trie only matches from the start of the string.
Weak answers forget that precomputed top-k in a trie means static ranking.
Weak answers ignore filters (category, locale, permissions) which inverted indexes handle naturally.

questions.q: Design a distributed rate limiter.
questions.answer:
**I use a token bucket per client key stored in a sharded Redis, updated atomically by a Lua script in one round trip from the API gateway or sidecar. Rules come from a config service; the limiter fails open with a local per-instance fallback when Redis is unavailable, and over-limit requests get 429 with Retry-After.**

**Clarify**: what is the key (user, API key, IP, tenant, endpoint), what limits (100/s with bursts of 200, 10k/day), how accurate (is a few percent overshoot fine?), and the latency budget (about 1 ms).

**Estimates**: 1M requests/s means 1M limiter checks/s; a Redis node does on the order of 100k simple operations per second, so a cluster of tens of shards keyed by client id; 10M keys at about 100 bytes is around 1 GB.

```text
 client -> LB -> gateway/sidecar --allow(key, cost)--> Redis Cluster (Lua token bucket)
                    |  local limiter (coarse fallback, hot-key shield)
```
